diagnosis_explanation: Your uterus had bad bleeding that did not get better with medicine. This caused a low red blood cell count. You also have fibroids in your uterus. These are growths that can cause problems. You also have a condition called adenomyosis. This means some uterine lining grew into the muscle wall of your uterus.
medication_rationale:
Motrin 600 mg:
This medicine is a pain reliever. It can help with cramps.
You may feel less pain when it works.
Some people get an upset stomach. This is common.
Call your doctor if you get a rash or feel short of breath.

Colace 100 mg:
This medicine helps soften your stools. It makes going to the bathroom easier.
You should have softer bowel movements.
Some people get mild stomach cramps. This is not usually a problem.
Call your doctor if you have severe stomach pain.

Ferrous Sulfate 60 mg:
This medicine gives your body iron. You may need more iron due to blood loss.
It helps your body make more red blood cells.
Your stools may turn dark or black. This is normal.
Call your doctor if you get bad stomach pain or feel very sick.

Multiple Vitamin:
This medicine gives your body vitamins and minerals. It helps keep you healthy.
You should not notice much change.
Some people get an upset stomach. Taking it with food can help.
Call your doctor if you get a rash or have trouble breathing.
recovery_trajectory:
**Week 1:**
- You will feel tired and sore after your surgery. This is normal.
- Rest in bed for the first week.
- Do not lift anything heavier than 5 pounds.
- You can eat your regular diet.
- Call your doctor if you have a fever over 100.4 F.
- Call your doctor if you have heavy bleeding.
- Your goal is to rest and let your body heal.

**Week 2:**
- Your pain should start to get a little better.
- You can slowly start moving around your house more.
- Continue to avoid lifting anything heavy.
- Keep eating your regular diet.
- Call your doctor if your pain gets worse.
- Your goal is to walk a short distance inside your home each day.

**Week 3:**
- You may start to feel more energy this week.
- You can do light chores like folding laundry.
- Do not lift anything heavier than 5 pounds.
- Keep eating your regular diet.
- Call your doctor if you see a lot of blood clots.
- Your goal is to walk for 10 minutes, twice a day.

**Week 4:**
- You should feel stronger and have more energy.
- You can increase your walking time slowly.
- Avoid any strenuous activity or heavy lifting.
- Continue with your regular diet.
- Call your doctor if you have bad belly pain.
- Your goal is to walk for 15 minutes each day.

**Week 5:**
- You can start to return to more normal activities.
- Still avoid lifting anything heavy or strenuous exercise.
- Keep eating your regular diet.
- Your goal is to walk for 20 minutes each day.
- Call your doctor if you have any concerns about healing.

**Week 6:**
- You should be able to do most normal daily activities.
- Slowly add back light exercise as you feel able.
- Keep avoiding heavy lifting for now.
- Continue eating your regular diet.
- Your goal is to walk for 30 minutes each day.
- Call your doctor if you have any unexpected symptoms.

**When to expect improvement:**
- You should feel much better in 4 to 6 weeks.
- Healing takes time, so be patient with yourself.
- Continue to listen to your body and rest when needed.
- Slowly get back to your normal activities.
escalation_guide:
CALL 911 IMMEDIATELY
These symptoms are life-threatening. Do not drive yourself.
- Uncontrolled bleeding: Bleeding can be severe.
- Heavy bleeding: You may soak a pad in one hour.
- Blood clots larger than a quarter: This means heavy bleeding.
- Feeling faint or dizzy: You may be losing too much blood.
- Trouble breathing: This can be a sign of shock.
- Chest pain or pressure: This needs heart care now.
- Sudden confusion: This is a sign of stroke.
- Not able to stay awake: This needs urgent care.

GO TO THE ER TODAY
Do not wait until tomorrow. Go within a few hours.
- Bleeding that soaks a pad in one hour: You are losing too much blood.
- Large blood clots: These mean very heavy bleeding.
- Pain that does not stop: Pain can mean problems.
- Fever over 101 degrees F: You may have an infection.
- Feeling sick to your stomach and vomiting: You cannot keep fluids down.
- Trouble urinating: You may have a blockage.
- Feeling weak or tired and cannot get up: This may mean more anemia.

CALL YOUR DOCTOR
Call during office hours. Do not go to the ER for these.
- Questions about your medicine: Your nurse can help you plan.
- Mild pain that is getting better: Pain should not be severe.
- Feeling tired but able to do daily tasks: This can happen with anemia.
- Feeling a little bit dizzy sometimes: Dizziness may get better.
- Mild nausea that comes and goes: Nausea can improve.
